subjects.name: Eiffel Tower
clues: This iron lattice structure was meant to stand for only twenty years.
It was built as the entrance arch to the 1889 World's Fair.
Its engineer's company also built the inner frame of the Statue of Liberty.
It is repainted about every seven years, using some 60 tonnes of paint.
The tallest landmark on the Champ de Mars in the French capital.
subjects.fact: It grows about 15 cm taller in summer heat.

subjects.name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
clues: Building it took almost 200 years, with long pauses during wars.
Soft ground on one side made it start to tilt while it was still being built.
Engineers straightened it by about 45 cm in work finished in 2001.
It is the bell tower of a cathedral in a Tuscan city.
Tourists pose as if holding up this famously tilted Italian bell tower.
subjects.fact: Legend says Galileo dropped balls from it to test falling speeds, though he may never have done so.

subjects.name: CN Tower
clues: It was built to send TV and radio signals over a growing city.
For over 30 years it was the tallest free-standing structure in the world.
It stands 553 metres tall, including its antenna.
Its glass floor and outdoor EdgeWalk let visitors look straight down from over 340 m.
This needle-like tower rises over Toronto on the shore of Lake Ontario.
subjects.fact: It is struck by lightning dozens of times a year.

subjects.name: Big Ben
clues: Strictly speaking, its famous name belongs to the great bell inside, not the tower.
Its tower was renamed in 2012 to honour a queen's Diamond Jubilee.
Its great bell weighs more than 13 tonnes.
It stands at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, beside the Thames.
London's most famous clock tower, whose chimes ring in the New Year on British TV.
subjects.fact: Old pennies placed on its pendulum are used to fine-tune the clock's timekeeping.

subjects.name: Burj Khalifa
clues: Its Y-shaped floor plan was inspired by a desert flower, the spider lily.
It is named after the leader of the UAE who helped fund its completion.
Tom Cruise climbed its outside in the film Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol.
It has held the title of the world's tallest building since it opened in 2010.
This 828-metre skyscraper towers over Dubai.
subjects.fact: Its tip can be seen from about 95 km away.

subjects.name: Golden Gate Bridge
clues: When it opened in 1937 it had the longest main span of any suspension bridge.
Its colour is officially called 'International Orange'.
It spans the strait linking a famous bay to the Pacific Ocean.
Its towers often seem to float above thick sea fog.
This orange-red suspension bridge is the symbol of San Francisco.
subjects.fact: Its towers rise about 227 metres above the water.

subjects.name: Tower Bridge
clues: It opened in 1894 after eight years of construction.
Its road deck splits in two and lifts to let tall ships pass.
Its high-level walkways now have glass floors for visitors.
It is often mistaken for London Bridge, its plainer neighbour upstream.
This twin-towered drawbridge crosses the Thames beside the Tower of London.
subjects.fact: In 1952 a bus had to jump the gap when the bridge began to open beneath it.

subjects.name: Brooklyn Bridge
clues: When it opened in 1883 it was the longest suspension bridge in the world.
After its chief engineer fell ill, his wife Emily Roebling oversaw much of the work.
In 1884 P. T. Barnum led 21 elephants across it to prove it was safe.
Its Gothic stone towers hold up steel cables over the East River.
This bridge links Manhattan with a neighbouring borough of New York City.
subjects.fact: It was the first suspension bridge to use steel-wire cables.

subjects.name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
clues: Opened in 1932, its steel arch earned it the nickname 'the Coathanger'.
It is one of the widest long-span bridges in the world, carrying trains, cars and walkers.
Visitors can climb over the top of its arch on guided tours.
Fireworks pour off it every New Year's Eve.
This steel arch bridge stands near the Opera House in Australia's oldest city.
subjects.fact: Its arch rises or falls by up to about 18 cm as the steel heats and cools.

subjects.name: Buckingham Palace
clues: It began as a large townhouse built for a duke in 1703.
Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live there, from 1837.
It has 775 rooms, including 19 state rooms.
Crowds gather outside it to watch the Changing of the Guard.
The London home of the British monarch, with a famous balcony.

links.name: United Kingdom
links.rel: is the royal home of the

subjects.fact: When the monarch is in residence, the Royal Standard flies above it.

subjects.name: Palace of Versailles
clues: It grew from a royal hunting lodge into one of the largest palaces in the world.
Its vast formal gardens were designed by André Le Nôtre.
The treaty ending the First World War was signed in its Hall of Mirrors in 1919.
King Louis XIV moved the royal court there in 1682.
This grand palace near Paris was the home of Marie Antoinette.
subjects.fact: Its Hall of Mirrors has 357 mirrors.

subjects.name: Forbidden City
clues: It was completed in 1420 under the Ming dynasty.
It was home to 24 emperors over nearly 500 years.
Ordinary people were not allowed to enter it without the emperor's permission.
Today it is a museum holding more than a million treasures.
This vast walled palace complex lies at the heart of Beijing.
subjects.fact: Legend says it has 9,999 and a half rooms; the true count is lower.

subjects.name: Alhambra
clues: Its name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'the red one'.
It was built mainly by the Nasrid dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Its Court of the Lions has a fountain held up by twelve stone lions.
It was the seat of the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, which surrendered in 1492.
This hilltop palace and fortress overlooks the city of Granada in Spain.
subjects.fact: Its intricate tile patterns inspired the artist M. C. Escher.

subjects.name: St. Peter's Basilica
clues: It was consecrated in 1626 after more than a century of building.
Michelangelo designed its great dome.
Bernini's bronze canopy stands over its main altar.
It is traditionally believed to stand over the tomb of Jesus's chief apostle.
This vast church in Vatican City faces a square where crowds gather to see the Pope.
subjects.fact: It is one of the largest churches in the world.

subjects.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
clues: Building began in 1163 and took nearly two centuries.
Victor Hugo's 1831 novel about its bell-ringer made it world-famous.
A fire in April 2019 destroyed its roof and wooden spire.
It reopened in December 2024 after five years of restoration.
This Gothic cathedral stands on the Île de la Cité in the French capital.
subjects.fact: Road distances in France are measured from a bronze star, 'point zéro', on the square in front of it.

subjects.name: St. Basil's Cathedral
clues: It was built in the 1550s on the orders of Ivan the Terrible.
It celebrated the capture of the city of Kazan in 1552.
Legend claims its architect was blinded so he could never build anything as beautiful.
Its swirling, brightly coloured onion domes look like flames of candy.
This cathedral with colourful onion domes stands on Red Square in Moscow.
subjects.fact: It has served mainly as a museum since the 1920s.

subjects.name: Sagrada Família
clues: Construction began in 1882 and was still going on more than 140 years later.
Its architect worked on it for over 40 years and is buried in its crypt.
It has been paid for by private donations and visitors' tickets.
Its tallest tower, dedicated to Jesus Christ, was designed to reach 172.5 metres.
Antoni Gaudí's unfinished basilica is the most famous sight in Barcelona.
subjects.fact: Gaudí is said to have joked about the slow progress: 'My client is not in a hurry.'

subjects.name: Sydney Opera House
clues: Its Danish architect, Jørn Utzon, left the project in 1966 and never saw it finished.
It was formally opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1973.
Its roof shells are covered with more than a million white and cream tiles.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
This sail-roofed performing arts centre stands on Bennelong Point near the Harbour Bridge.
subjects.fact: It cost about 14 times its original budget.

subjects.name: White House
clues: Every president since John Adams has lived there.
British troops set it on fire in 1814.
Its Oval Office is where the president usually works.
Its address is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.
The official home of the President of the United States in Washington, D.C.

links.name: United States
links.rel: is the presidential home of the

subjects.fact: It has 132 rooms and 35 bathrooms.

subjects.name: Louvre
clues: It began as a fortress built around 1200 by King Philip II.
It opened as a public museum in 1793, during the French Revolution.
A glass pyramid designed by I. M. Pei became its main entrance in 1989.
It is the most visited art museum in the world.
This former royal palace in Paris displays the Mona Lisa.
subjects.fact: In 1911 the Mona Lisa was stolen from it and was missing for over two years.

subjects.name: Empire State Building
clues: It went up in just over a year and opened in 1931.
It was the tallest skyscraper in the world for nearly 40 years.
Its top is lit in different colours to mark holidays and events.
The giant ape King Kong climbed it in the 1933 film.
This Art Deco skyscraper on Fifth Avenue is New York City's most famous.
subjects.fact: It has its own ZIP code, 10118.

subjects.name: Taj Mahal
clues: Around 20,000 workers built it over some 20 years.
Its white marble seems to change from pink at dawn to gold at sunset.
Emperor Shah Jahan built it in memory of his beloved wife, who died in 1631.
It stands on the bank of the Yamuna River in Agra.
This white marble tomb is the most famous building in India.
subjects.fact: It was named one of the New 7 Wonders of the World in 2007.

subjects.name: Arc de Triomphe
clues: Napoleon ordered it in 1806 after his victory at Austerlitz.
It was finally completed in 1836, long after the death of the man who ordered it.
The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier from the First World War lies beneath it.
Twelve avenues radiate from the star-shaped square around it.
This giant arch stands at the top of the Champs-Élysées in Paris.
subjects.fact: In 1919 a pilot flew a biplane straight through it.

subjects.name: Mount Rushmore
clues: Carving began in 1927 and stopped in 1941.
About 400 workers used dynamite to blast away most of the rock.
Each of its faces is about 18 metres tall.
Its sculptor, Gutzon Borglum, died months before the work ended.
Four presidents' faces are carved into this mountain in South Dakota.
subjects.fact: A hidden 'Hall of Records' chamber lies behind the carved faces.

subjects.name: Great Wall of China
clues: Its many sections, built over some 2,000 years, add up to more than 20,000 km.
Most of its best-preserved parts were built during the Ming dynasty.
Contrary to popular belief, it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
It was built to protect against raids by nomadic peoples from the north.
This ancient defensive barrier snakes over the mountains north of Beijing.
subjects.fact: Sticky rice was mixed into the mortar of some of its later sections.

subjects.name: Statue of Liberty
clues: It was a gift from the people of France, dedicated in 1886.
Its copper skin has slowly turned green over time.
The tablet in its left hand is inscribed with the date July 4, 1776.
It was sculpted by Bartholdi, and Gustave Eiffel designed its inner frame.
This torch-bearing statue greets ships in New York Harbor.
subjects.fact: The seven rays of its crown are said to stand for the seven seas and continents.

subjects.name: Christ the Redeemer
clues: It was completed in 1931 after nine years of work.
Its outer layer is a mosaic of thousands of small soapstone tiles.
It is about 30 metres tall, with arms stretching 28 metres wide.
It stands on top of Corcovado mountain, about 700 metres above the city.
This giant statue of Jesus with outstretched arms overlooks Rio de Janeiro.
subjects.fact: It is struck by lightning several times a year.

subjects.name: Great Sphinx of Giza
clues: It was carved straight out of the limestone bedrock.
It is about 73 metres long and 20 metres high.
Its missing nose has inspired many legends.
It has the body of a lion and the head of a man, thought to be a pharaoh.
This lion-bodied statue guards the pyramids on the edge of Cairo.
subjects.fact: It is thought to be the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt.

subjects.name: Moai
clues: Nearly 1,000 of them were carved by the Rapa Nui people.
Most were carved from volcanic stone at the Rano Raraku quarry.
Some wear huge red stone hats called pukao.
Many stand with their backs to the sea, facing inland.
These giant stone heads and torsos stand on Easter Island, part of Chile.
subjects.fact: Some that look like just heads have bodies buried underground.

subjects.name: Colosseum
clues: It opened in AD 80 with games said to have lasted 100 days.
It could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators.
Its name may come from a colossal statue of Emperor Nero that stood nearby.
Gladiators fought wild animals and each other in its oval arena.
This huge ruined amphitheatre stands in the heart of Rome.
subjects.fact: It was named one of the New 7 Wonders of the World in 2007.

subjects.name: Machu Picchu
clues: It was built around 1450 for an Inca emperor.
It was abandoned about a century later, around the time of the Spanish conquest.
Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911.
Many visitors reach it by hiking the Inca Trail.
This Inca citadel sits high on a mountain ridge in Peru's Andes.
subjects.fact: Its stone walls were built without mortar, the blocks fitted tightly together.

subjects.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
clues: It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one still standing.
For nearly 4,000 years it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth.
It is made of an estimated 2.3 million stone blocks.
It was built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC.
The largest of three famous royal tombs on a plateau near Cairo.
subjects.fact: Its four sides are lined up almost exactly with north, south, east and west.

subjects.name: Stonehenge
clues: Some of its stones were hauled over 200 km from the hills of Wales.
Its biggest stones were raised around 2500 BC.
At the summer solstice the sun rises in line with its entrance.
Its huge sarsen stones are topped by horizontal lintels.
This prehistoric ring of standing stones lies on Salisbury Plain in England.
subjects.fact: In 2024 scientists found that its Altar Stone came from north-east Scotland.

subjects.name: Parthenon
clues: Its columns bulge slightly in the middle so they look perfectly straight from afar.
A gunpowder explosion in 1687 blew off its roof.
Built in the 400s BC, it was dedicated to the goddess Athena.
Many of its marble sculptures are displayed in the British Museum.
This columned temple crowns the Acropolis of Athens.
subjects.fact: Over its life it has been a temple, a church, a mosque and a gunpowder store.

subjects.name: Chichen Itza
clues: It was one of the largest Maya cities, at its height about a thousand years ago.
Its main pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps, one for each day of the year.
At the spring and autumn equinoxes a shadow serpent seems to slither down its pyramid.
It was named one of the New 7 Wonders of the World in 2007.
This ancient Maya city lies on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.
subjects.fact: Clapping in front of its main pyramid makes an echo said to sound like a bird's chirp.

subjects.name: Angkor Wat
clues: It is often called the largest religious monument in the world.
It was built in the early 1100s as a Hindu temple and later became Buddhist.
It was the great temple of the Khmer Empire.
Its towers appear on its country's national flag.
This vast temple complex near Siem Reap is Cambodia's best-known sight.
subjects.fact: Unusually for temples of its kind, it faces west.

subjects.name: Mount Everest
clues: Its height was remeasured in 2020 at 8,848.86 metres.
Its summit is made of limestone that once lay on an ancient seabed.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached its top in 1953.
It sits on the border between Nepal and China, in the Himalayas.
This is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level.
subjects.fact: Climbers call the thin-aired zone above 8,000 metres 'the death zone'.

subjects.name: Mount Kilimanjaro
clues: It is made of three volcanic cones: Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.
Its highest point, Uhuru Peak, is about 5,895 metres above sea level.
It is often called the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.
Its shrinking glaciers sit just south of the equator.
This snow-capped volcano in Tanzania is the highest mountain in Africa.
subjects.fact: Climbers pass through several climate zones, from farmland to an arctic summit.

subjects.name: Mount Fuji
clues: This volcano last erupted in 1707.
It stands 3,776 metres tall.
Its near-perfect cone appears in Hokusai's famous woodblock prints.
Its climbing season usually runs in July and August.
Japan's highest mountain, a snow-capped volcano visible from Tokyo.
subjects.fact: The upper part of the mountain is owned by a Shinto shrine.

subjects.name: Matterhorn
clues: It was first climbed in 1865, and four of the seven climbers died on the way down.
It rises to 4,478 metres in the Alps.
Its four steep faces point roughly north, south, east and west.
Its outline appeared on Toblerone chocolate packaging for decades.
This pyramid-shaped peak on the Swiss-Italian border towers over Zermatt.
subjects.fact: Disneyland has had a smaller copy of it since 1959.

subjects.name: Amazon River
clues: It carries more water than any other river on Earth.
No bridge crosses its main stream.
Its waters are home to pink river dolphins and piranhas.
It flows from the Andes of Peru east to the Atlantic Ocean.
This mighty South American river runs through the world's largest rainforest.
subjects.fact: About a fifth of all the river water reaching the world's oceans comes from it.

subjects.name: Nile
clues: It is one of the two longest rivers in the world.
Its two main branches are called the White and the Blue.
Those two branches meet at Khartoum in Sudan.
Its yearly floods made farming possible for the ancient Egyptians.
This river flows north through Egypt and Cairo to the Mediterranean.
subjects.fact: Its basin covers parts of 11 countries.

subjects.name: Mississippi River
clues: It starts as a small stream flowing out of Lake Itasca in Minnesota.
Mark Twain worked as a steamboat pilot on it.
It flows south past St. Louis, Memphis and New Orleans.
It ends in a bird's-foot-shaped delta south of New Orleans.
Huckleberry Finn rafts down this great river of the central United States.
subjects.fact: Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great river'.

subjects.name: Danube
clues: It flows through or along ten countries, more than any other river.
It begins in Germany's Black Forest.
Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade all stand on its banks.
It empties into the Black Sea through a wide delta, mostly in Romania.
Europe's second-longest river, it is honoured in a famous Strauss waltz.
subjects.fact: Four national capitals lie on it, more than on any other river.

subjects.name: Niagara Falls
clues: It is made up of three waterfalls on the border of two countries.
Its largest part is called the Horseshoe Falls.
In 1901 Annie Edson Taylor went over it in a barrel and survived.
Boats carry visitors right up to its thundering spray.
These famous falls lie on the border between Canada and the United States.
subjects.fact: At night much of its water is diverted to make electricity.

subjects.name: Victoria Falls
clues: It is often called the largest sheet of falling water in the world.
Its spray can be seen from many kilometres away.
Its local name means 'the Smoke that Thunders'.
The explorer David Livingstone named it after a British queen in 1855.
This wide waterfall on the Zambezi River lies between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
subjects.fact: In the dry season, swimmers can sit in the 'Devil's Pool' right at its edge.

subjects.name: Angel Falls
clues: It plunges from the top of a flat-topped jungle mountain called a tepui.
It is named after an American pilot who flew over it in the 1930s.
It inspired Paradise Falls in the Pixar film Up.
It drops 979 metres, the highest unbroken fall of water on Earth.
This record-breaking waterfall is in Venezuela's Canaima National Park.
subjects.fact: Much of its water turns to mist before it reaches the bottom.

subjects.name: Iguazu Falls
clues: It is made up of around 275 separate drops along nearly 3 km.
Its name comes from Guaraní words meaning 'big water'.
Its most famous section is the U-shaped 'Devil's Throat'.
On seeing it, Eleanor Roosevelt reportedly exclaimed 'Poor Niagara!'
This vast system of waterfalls lies on the border of Argentina and Brazil.
subjects.fact: Both sides of the falls are protected as national parks and UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

subjects.name: Grand Canyon
clues: It was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years.
Its rock layers reveal nearly two billion years of Earth's history.
It is about 446 km long and more than 1.8 km deep in places.
A glass Skywalk juts out over its edge on Hualapai land.
This huge red-rock gorge is the most famous national park in Arizona.
subjects.fact: It became a national park in 1919.

subjects.name: Sahara
clues: Its name comes from the Arabic word for 'desert'.
Only about a quarter of it is covered by sand dunes.
Several thousand years ago much of it was green grassland with lakes.
It covers most of North Africa, from the Atlantic to the Red Sea.
This is the largest hot desert in the world.
subjects.fact: Some of its sand dunes are taller than 180 metres.

subjects.name: Great Barrier Reef
clues: It is made up of nearly 3,000 separate coral systems and hundreds of islands.
It stretches for over 2,300 km through the Coral Sea.
It is the largest structure built by living things on Earth.
Warming seas have caused mass coral bleaching there.
This vast coral wonder lies off the coast of Queensland, Australia.
subjects.fact: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

subjects.name: Uluru
clues: It rises about 348 metres above the flat plain around it.
Much of its bulk is believed to lie hidden underground.
It glows red and orange at sunrise and sunset.
Climbing it was banned in 2019 out of respect for its Anangu owners.
This huge sandstone monolith stands in the red centre of Australia.
subjects.fact: Its English name honoured Henry Ayers, a 19th-century premier of South Australia.
